result:
There is a particular kind of silence that arrives just before rain.

It is not the absence of sound. Leaves still move. Cars continue along wet-looking streets that are not yet wet. Somewhere, a screen door closes, a dog barks, and someone remembers they left laundry outside. But everything seems to pause at the edge of itself, as if the world has taken a breath and has not decided when to let it go.

Then the first drop falls.

It darkens a coin-sized patch of pavement. Another lands beside it. Soon the ground is stippled with small, temporary shadows, each one joining the next until the whole street changes color.

Rain is ordinary, which may be why it is easy to love. It asks for no interpretation. It does not care whether the day has gone well. It falls on celebrations and arguments, on empty parking lots, on gardens tended carefully and weeds growing through concrete. It makes roofs speak. It gathers at curbs and carries away dust, petals, wrappers, and tiny forgotten things.

For a few minutes, everyone belongs to the same weather.

People hurry beneath awnings. Cyclists lower their heads. Children jump into puddles with the solemn commitment of explorers. Inside, kettles are filled. Windows become more interesting than televisions. Familiar rooms feel briefly sheltered, not merely enclosed.

And then, eventually, the rain weakens. The separate drops become countable again. Gutters quiet. Birds resume their conversations as if they had only been waiting for a difficult speaker to finish.

The world after rain is not new, exactly. The cracks remain. The errands remain. Whatever worried us before the storm is probably still there.

But the air has changed, and sometimes that is enough.
